No equivalence is asserted, so there is no reverse direction to check.

citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write $$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$ This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in $\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index. The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient norm values are supplied by [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]] for real scalars and [[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars. Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$, there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying $$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$ Here the weak derivative is the one in [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under [[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and invariance under null-set changes follow from [[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while [[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the $L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class, denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation. For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$, $$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$ The Sobolev norm expression is $$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$ The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and $\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression. The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition. For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in $\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such $U$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

**(a) Framework data.** Adopt the framework data of clause (a) of the declared central-potential model [[def-nrqm-central-framework-central-potential-model]] with a declared mass parameter $m>0$, spin label $s=0$, the state space $H_{0}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$, the componentwise position and momentum families and the action constant $\hbar>0$ of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]]; units are those of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice as the choice hypotheses of the cited mathematical suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). **(b) The declared one-centre Coulomb model.** As an additional model assumption of the pair, fix a real **coupling** $\kappa>0$ with the declared unit $\mathrm{J\,m}$ and put $$\gamma:=\frac{2m\kappa}{\hbar^{2}}\qquad(\text{unit }\mathrm{m^{-1}}),\qquad C_{\gamma}:=-\Delta-\frac{\gamma}{|\cdot|}\ \text{ on }\ D(C_{\gamma})=H^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C),$$ the self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] clause (c). The **assigned energy operator** of the one-centre Coulomb model is $$H_{\kappa}:=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\,C_{\gamma},$$ with domain $D(H_{\kappa}):=D(C_{\gamma})$; by [[lem-nrqm-potentials-positive-scaling-of-self-adjoint-operators]] clauses (a) and (b) it is self-adjoint with the same domain, and by [[lem-nrqm-central-free-operator-differential-identification]] together with the action formula of the cited theorem it acts by $$H_{\kappa}f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f-\kappa\frac{f}{|\cdot|}\qquad(f\in D(H_{\kappa})),$$ where $\Delta_{w}$ is the weak Laplacian. The model declares the **length scale** $a_{\kappa}:=\hbar^{2}/(m\kappa)$, read in metres, and the **energy scale** $\mathcal E_{\kappa}:=m\kappa^{2}/(2\hbar^{2})=\hbar^{2}/(2ma_{\kappa}^{2})$, read in joules. The model adopts $(H_{\kappa},\mathrm J)$ as its declared energy observable for the one-centre problem; the self-adjointness is the cited theorem's and no spectral property is presupposed here. **(c) The declared radial reading of the one-centre model.** Let $U$ and $(A_{l})_{l\ge0}$ be the unitary and the radial operators of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] clauses (a)-(d): $U$ maps $H_{0}$ onto $K=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^{2}((0,\infty),dr;\mathbb C)$ with $UH_{\kappa}U^{*}=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}(\hbar^{2}/2m)A_{l}$, and each $A_{l}$ is self-adjoint with form domain $V_{l}$ and domain $D(A_{l})$. The model declares the **sector $(l,m)$ radial energy operator** $A_{l}^{(\kappa)}:=(\hbar^{2}/2m)A_{l}$, read in joules, and, for a class $u\in D(A_{l})$, the **declared radial equation** is the distributional identity $$-u''(r)+\Bigl(\frac{l(l+1)}{r^{2}}-\frac{\gamma}{r}\Bigr)u(r)=A_{l}u(r)\qquad\text{on }(0,\infty),$$ which by clause (c) of the cited theorem is an ordinary differential equation with $C^{2}$ representative whenever $A_{l}u=Eu$ for a constant $E$. The **regular reduced solution** at energy attribute $k>0$ is the function $u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)=r^{l+1}e^{-kr}v(2kr)$ of clause (c) of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-kummer-recurrence-and-termination]], with $v$ the regular power series of that clause; the pair uses it as the declared radial template of the model, not as a physical state, until the normalisation and spectral theorems of the page identify it. **(d) The declared two-body Coulomb model.** As a further model assumption, take two **distinguishable** spinless massive particles with declared mass parameters $m_{1},m_{2}>0$ (unit kg) and opposite declared charges: particle 1 carries $-q$ and particle 2 carries $+q$, with a real **charge parameter** $q>0$ (unit C). Declare the **pair coupling** $$\kappa:=\frac{q^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}},\qquad \varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1},$$ where $\mu_{0}$ is the declared magnetic constant of the SI conventions and $c$ the speed of light, both as in clause (c) of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]; the identification $\kappa=q^{2}/(4\pi\varepsilon_{0})$ is a constitutive assumption of the model, and $\kappa$ is read in $\mathrm{J\,m}$. The two-particle state space is the Hilbert tensor product of two copies of the one-particle space of clause (a) as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], identified with $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{6};\mathbb C)$ through [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]]; the spin-zero internal factor is trivial, and because the two particles are of different species no symmetrisation is imposed (the case of identical species belongs to the identical-particle sector of P6 and is not used here). The **assigned energy operator** is $$H_{2}:=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{1}}\Delta_{x_{1}}-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{2}}\Delta_{x_{2}}-\frac{\kappa}{|x_{1}-x_{2}|},\qquad D(H_{2}):=H^{2}(\mathbb R^{6};\mathbb C),$$ which is self-adjoint by clause (c) of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-two-body-reduced-mass]]. Let $$\Phi(x_{1},x_{2}):=(R,r),\qquad R:=\frac{m_{1}x_{1}+m_{2}x_{2}}{M},\quad r:=x_{1}-x_{2},\quad M:=m_{1}+m_{2},$$ be the centre-of-mass/relative coordinate map of that theorem, with its unitary $U_{\Phi}$. The model declares the **centre-of-mass/relative reading** $U_{\Phi}H_{2}U_{\Phi}^{-1}=T_{R}\otimes I+I\otimes C_{\mu}$ of clause (c) of that theorem, with the **reduced mass** $$\mu:=\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\qquad(\text{unit }\mathrm{kg}),$$ the centre-of-mass kinetic operator $T_{R}:=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2M}\Delta_{R}$ and the **relative operator** $C_{\mu}:=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2\mu}\Delta_{r}-\frac{\kappa}{|r|}$; the relative operator is exactly the one-centre Coulomb operator of clause (b) with mass parameter $\mu$. The model further declares the **fixed-nucleus reading**: the one-centre model of clauses (b), (c) with mass parameter $m_{1}$ is read as the limiting description in which the second particle is infinitely heavy, $\mu\to m_{1}$ as $m_{2}\to\infty$ at fixed $m_{1},\kappa$; this is a declared limiting reading, and no convergence theorem for operators or states is asserted by it. **(e) The hydrogen-like identification.** A **hydrogen-like ion** assignment of the two-body model is the choice $m_{1}=m_{\mathrm e}$ (electron mass parameter), $m_{2}=m_{\mathrm n}$ (nuclear mass parameter) and $q=e$ (the elementary charge of clause (c) of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]) with nuclear charge $+Ze$, so that $\kappa=Ze^{2}/(4\pi\varepsilon_{0})$ for a declared positive integer $Z$; $Z=1$ with a proton mass parameter $m_{\mathrm p}$ is the **hydrogen assignment**. These assignments use empirical mass and charge parameters; any comparison of the model's consequences with a laboratory hydrogen atom is a tested identification in the sense of clause (iii) of P7 ([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]) and carries the uncertainty of that identification. The model declares no numerical value of $m_{\mathrm e},m_{\mathrm n},e,\mu_{0}$ or $\hbar$; numerical evaluations, when made, use their declared or measured values as explicitly qualified empirical inputs. **(f) Scope exclusions.** Until their own items introduce them, the Coulomb and hydrogen models exclude: spin, magnetic moment couplings and spin–statistics assignments beyond the trivial spin-zero factor; relativistic corrections, in particular any fine-structure splitting of the degeneracy of the gross-structure levels; finite nuclear size, nuclear recoil beyond the two-body reduction of clause (d), and nuclear structure; QED corrections such as vacuum polarisation and the Lamb shift, and hyperfine structure; shielding and many-body modification of the $1/r$ potential; the radiation extension, spontaneous emission, radiation reaction and any photon, transition-frequency or line-intensity statement; external electromagnetic fields; and any scattering, ionisation or continuum process, which belongs to the scattering items of the quantum-mechanics track. The model asserts no empirical result and fixes no measured quantity.

Adopt the framework postulates P1, P2, P4 and P5 and the readings of the declared one-centre Coulomb model [[def-nrqm-central-framework-coulomb-and-hydrogen-model]] clauses (a)-(c) with parameters $\hbar>0$, $m>0$ and coupling $\kappa>0$, its assigned energy operator $H_{\kappa}$ with length scale $a_{\kappa}=\hbar^{2}/(m\kappa)$, and the energy-observable content of [[pthm-nrqm-central-coulomb-energy-observable-and-flow]] ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]], [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]], [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]], [[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]], [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]], [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For $n\ge1$, $0\le l\le n-1$, $-l\le m\le l$ let $\psi_{nlm}$ be the regular bound solutions of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-negative-subspace-completeness-and-degeneracy]] and put $\Psi_{nlm}:=\psi_{nlm}/\|\psi_{nlm}\|$, and put $$E_{n}:=-\frac{m\kappa^{2}}{2\hbar^{2}n^{2}}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2ma_{\kappa}^{2}n^{2}}\qquad(n\ge1).$$ Then: (a) for every label, $\Psi_{nlm}\in D(H_{\kappa})$, $\|\Psi_{nlm}\|=1$, $H_{\kappa}\Psi_{nlm}=E_{n}\Psi_{nlm}$, and vectors with distinct labels are orthogonal; the vectors $\Psi_{nlm}$ of fixed $n$ span a subspace of dimension $\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}(2l+1)=n^{2}$; (b) the eigenvalues of $H_{\kappa}$ are exactly the numbers $E_{n}$, $n\ge1$; the eigenspace of $H_{\kappa}$ at $E_{n}$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\Psi_{nlm}:0\le l\le n-1,\ -l\le m\le l\}$, so the model assigns to the level $n$ the **model degeneracy** $n^{2}$; in particular $H_{\kappa}$ has no eigenvalues in $[0,+\infty)$, whose spectral content is entirely essential spectrum $[0,+\infty)$ in the sense of [[pthm-nrqm-central-coulomb-energy-observable-and-flow]] (a); (c) the family $(\Psi_{nlm})_{n\ge1,\,0\le l\le n-1,\,-l\le m\le l}$ is a complete orthonormal family of the negative spectral subspace $E_{H_{\kappa}}((-\infty,0))L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$: the bound states span exactly the preparations whose energy outcomes are negative almost surely; (d) the family is not complete in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$: the nonnegative spectral subspace $E_{H_{\kappa}}([0,+\infty))L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ is nonzero, indeed infinite dimensional, and every unit vector $\psi$ in it has $\mu^{H_{\kappa}}_{\psi}(B)=0$ for every Borel $B\subseteq(-\infty,0)$, i.e. strictly negative energy outcomes have probability zero in such a preparation; consequently the bound states of the model do not exhaust its state space and the model possesses continuum states which are not bound states; (e) *Energy-law reading.* For every unit vector $\psi$ the restriction of the energy outcome law to the negative half-line is the discrete law $\sum_{n\ge1}w_{n}\delta_{E_{n}}$ with weights $w_{n}:=\|E_{H_{\kappa}}(\{E_{n}\})\psi\|^{2}\ge0$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}w_{n}=\|E_{H_{\kappa}}((-\infty,0))\psi\|^{2}\le1$; for $\psi=\Psi_{nlm}$ the whole law is the point mass $\delta_{E_{n}}$; (f) *Scope.* The statement is conditional on P1, P2, P4, P5, the declared Coulomb model and the cited mathematics. The values $E_{n}$ are model parameters determined by $\hbar,m,\kappa$; no numerical value, no measured line, no transition rate, no photon or light-matter coupling and no empirical result is asserted. The absolute continuity of the positive spectral subspace is recorded by the cited mathematics for the unscaled operator and is not restated for the scaled model here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Y:=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with its norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]), let $\gamma\in C^2([0,1];(0,\infty))$ with $0<\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma(s)\le\gamma_{\max}<\infty$, and put $$A(s):=-\Delta-\frac{\gamma(s)}{|\cdot|},\qquad D(A(s))=Y .$$ Fix $n\ge1$, let $P_n(s)$ be the spectral projection of $A(s)$ for the eigenvalue $E_n(s)=-\gamma(s)^2/(4n^2)$ and let $g_n:=\inf_{s\in[0,1]}\operatorname{dist}(E_n(s),\sigma(A(s))\setminus\{E_n(s)\})>0$ be the uniform gap to the rest of the spectrum. Let $U_T$ solve $i\,\partial_sU_T=T A(s)U_T$, $U_T(0)=I$ ([[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-common-domain-nonautonomous-evolution]], with $T$ a slow-time parameter). Then there is a constant $C<\infty$, depending on $n,\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}$ and the $C^2$ norm of $\gamma$, with $$\bigl\|(I-P_n(s))U_T(s)P_n(0)\bigr\|\le\frac CT,\qquad s\in[0,1].$$ The theorem is a conditional statement about the external-source Coulomb family $A(s)$; no laboratory control field, error rate or physical preparation is asserted, and linear Stark-type couplings are not covered.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $Y$ be a dense linear subspace of $H$ that is itself a Hilbert space continuously embedded in $H$ (for instance $Y=D(A_0)$ with the graph norm of a self-adjoint $A_0$), let $T>0$, and let $A(t)$ for $t\in[0,T]$ be an operator with $D(A(t))=Y$, self-adjoint as an operator on $H$, such that $t\mapsto A(t)$ belongs to $C^1([0,T];\mathcal B(Y,H))$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Put $L:=\sup_t\|A'(t)\|_{\mathcal B(Y,H)}$. Then: (a) *Existence and uniqueness of a strong propagator.* There is a family $U(t,s)$, $0\le s\le t\le T$, of unitary operators on $H$ with: $U(s,s)=I$; $U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)$; $(t,s)\mapsto U(t,s)\xi$ continuous on $\{s\le t\}$ for each $\xi\in H$; $U(t,s)Y=Y$ with $\|U(t,s)y\|_Y\le C_T\|y\|_Y$ for a constant $C_T$ independent of $(s,t)\in[0,T]^2$; and for every $y\in Y$ the map $t\mapsto U(t,s)y$ is $C^1$ in $H$ with $$i\,\partial_tU(t,s)y=A(t)U(t,s)y,\qquad s\le t\le T.$$ (b) *Uniqueness.* If $V(t,s)$ is another family of bounded linear operators on $H$ with the same strong equation on $Y$, $V(s,s)=I$ and $\sup_{r}\|V(r,s)y\|_{H}<\infty$, then $V=U$. (c) *Equations for the reverse and adjoint.* $U(t,s)Y=Y$ for all $0\le s\le t\le T$ and $U(s,t):=U(t,s)^{-1}$ satisfies $i\partial_sU(s,t)y=A(s)U(s,t)y$ for $y\in Y$; $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)$. Equivalently, differentiating the second argument of the forward propagator gives $i\partial_sU(t,s)y=-U(t,s)A(s)y$. The domain maps are jointly strongly continuous in $Y$. The theorem is stated for the abstract family $A$; a physical generator is obtained by $A=H_{\mathrm{energy}}/\hbar$ after choosing a time unit.

**(a) Framework data.** Adopt the framework data and readings of [[def-nrqm-driven-dynamics-framework-driven-model]] clauses (a), (d) (P1, P2 and P4 and their state, observable and evolution readings; units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]); assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral and evolution suppliers. The autonomous-dynamics postulate P4 is adopted in the reading of [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]]; the protocol below is the reading of its clause (iv) for slowly varying families. **(b) The declared slow family.** As an additional model assumption of the pair, fix a **protocol duration** $T>0$ (seconds), the **slow parameter** $s\in[0,1]$, and a family $s\mapsto H(s)$ of self-adjoint operators on the declared state space $\mathfrak H$ ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), read as the model's **energy at slow time $s$**, in one of the two declared regularity branches: - **(f) finite branch.** $\mathfrak H=\mathbb C^{d}$ for some $d\ge1$ and $H\in C^{2}([0,1];\operatorname{Herm}(\mathbb C^{d}))$; - **(u) common-domain branch.** $D(H(s))=Y$ for a dense subspace $Y\subseteq\mathfrak H$ that is a Hilbert space continuously embedded in $\mathfrak H$, every $H(s)$ is self-adjoint on $\mathfrak H$, and $s\mapsto H(s)$ is of class $C^{1}([0,1];\mathcal B(Y,\mathfrak H))$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]). The family is prescribed model data: no laboratory ramp, field source or feedback is assumed. The **protocol propagator** is the unique unitary family $U_{T}(s,\sigma)$ on $\mathfrak H$ solving the slow-time Schroedinger equation $$i\hbar\,\partial_{s}U_{T}(s,\sigma)=T\,H(s)U_{T}(s,\sigma),\qquad U_{T}(\sigma,\sigma)=I,\qquad 0\le\sigma\le s\le1,$$ whose existence is cited from the mathematics: in branch (f) the family $s\mapsto TH(s)/\hbar$ is norm-continuous with bounded self-adjoint values and $U_T$ is its Dyson propagator ([[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-norm-dyson-series-and-uniqueness]]), and in branch (u) the family $s\mapsto TH(s)/\hbar$ lies in $C^{1}([0,1];\mathcal B(Y,\mathfrak H))$ and $U_T$ is its strong propagator ([[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-common-domain-nonautonomous-evolution]]). The model's evolution in physical time is $\psi(t):=U_{T}(t/T,0)\psi(0)$ for $t\in[0,T]$, and the evolved preparation is $\rho(t):=U_{T}(t/T,0)\rho(0)U_{T}(t/T,0)^{*}$, read as in clause (d) of [[def-nrqm-driven-dynamics-framework-driven-model]]. **(c) Followed spectral subspace and uniform gap.** Fix a **label**: for branch (f) a spectral cluster $\sigma_{P}(s)\subseteq\sigma(H(s))$ ([[def-discrete-and-essential-spectrum-of-a-self-adjoint-operator]]) with spectral projection $P(s)$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and for branch (u) a fixed finite-multiplicity eigenvalue $E(s)$ of $H(s)$ with spectral projection $P(s)$. The label is declared **uniformly gapped** when $$\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\sigma_{P}(s),\,\sigma(H(s))\setminus\sigma_{P}(s)\bigr)\ge g>0\qquad(s\in[0,1])$$ in branch (f), respectively $\operatorname{dist}(E(s),\sigma(H(s))\setminus\{E(s)\})\ge g>0$ in branch (u), and **coherently followed** when $s\mapsto P(s)$ is continuous in operator norm and coincides with the local Riesz continuation of $P(0)$ (in branch (f): the spectral projection of $H(s)$ for the cluster continuously connected to the initial one). A **preparation in the subspace** is a preparation with $\rho(0)$ supported in $\operatorname{ran}P(0)$; for a unit vector $\psi(0)\in\operatorname{ran}P(0)$ the **leakage probability** at slow time $s$ is the model's outcome probability $$p_{\mathrm{leak}}(s):=\mu^{(I-P(s))}_{\psi(sT)}(\{1\})=\bigl\|(I-P(s))\psi(sT)\bigr\|^{2},\qquad \psi(sT)=U_{T}(s,0)\psi(0),$$ that is, the Born probability in the reading of P2 that the evolved preparation is found outside the followed subspace at slow time $s$ ([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]], [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]; [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]], [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]). **(d) Status and scope.** Clauses (b)-(c) adopt the protocol as an idealization and fix its vocabulary. The size of the leakage is not part of the definition: it is the content of the adiabatic theorems of the page, which are conditional on the uniform gap and on coherent following. The definition asserts no claim that a laboratory ramp realizes the family, no selection or relaxation of a branch by the protocol, no thermalization, no measurement record and no empirical result; whether a laboratory preparation realizes a preparation in the declared subspace is a tested identification in the sense of P7.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned sharp observable** of the system is a pair $(A,u_A)$ consisting of a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ on the assigned Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) and a **declared unit** $u_A$ in which the real spectral coordinate of $A$ is read, in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The domain $D(A)$ is part of the assignment: symmetry on a smaller domain, or a formal differential expression, does not by itself supply an assigned observable ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition. **(b) Spectral measure and outcome law.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral suppliers. The self-adjoint operator $A$ has a unique spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, with $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,x}<\infty\}$ and $Ax=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)x$, where $E_{A,x}(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment $$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$ the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b). **(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$, and an exact value of a quantity with no eigenvalues is an idealization outside the assignment, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2. **(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable. **(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation. **(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it. **(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below. **(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it. **(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$. **(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$. **(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). The existence of the completed tensor product is mathematics; the assignment of that product to a composite physical system is the physical assumption here. **(v) Restrictions that are separate assumptions.** Restrictions of the state space by superselection rules, identical-particle symmetry sectors, and the replacement of the tensor product by more general algebraic structures are not consequences of the clauses above: where such a restriction is used it is adopted separately, and the identical-species sectors are the subject of the postulate P6 of this page. **(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model within its declared sector. They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about sharp and unsharp real-valued quantities. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The latter is the explicit hypothesis used to obtain the spectral PVM of a general self-adjoint operator from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] in clause (ii); consumers invoking this construction inherit it. **(i) Sharp observables.** An **ideal sharp real-valued quantity** (observable) of a system with state space $H$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), together with a declared unit in which its real spectral coordinate is read; the unit is part of the assignment, and no numerical value of the coordinate is asserted by the assignment. Symmetry of $A$ on a small domain is not sufficient for self-adjointness, and the domain is a declared part of the observable. **(ii) Spectral probability.** Let $E_{A}$ be the spectral projection-valued measure of the self-adjoint operator $A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ the **probability of the outcome in $B$** is $$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{A}(B)\bigr),\qquad\text{and for a pure preparation }[\psi]\text{ it is }\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}.$$ By clause (b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] the assignment $B\mapsto\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets ([[def-probability-measure]], [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). It is the general form of the Born rule adopted here. **(iii) Nature of the outcome law.** The probability law is a measure, not necessarily a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and not necessarily a finite or countable sum of point masses: a self-adjoint operator with continuous spectrum ordinarily has no normalizable eigenvector at a point of its continuous spectrum, so an "exact value" of a continuum quantity is not represented by a normalized state. An ideal point value is an idealization; a real detector reports a finite-resolution outcome, that is, the probability of a declared Borel set $B$ such as a bin, and the recorded-event probability is that of (ii) for the bin, not the value of a density at a point. **(iv) Unsharp finite outcomes.** Outcomes of a finite-resolution apparatus with finitely many channels are described, when the idealization uses bounded effects, by a finite family $(F_{a})_{a=1}^{p}$ of bounded operators with $0\le F_{a}\le I$ in the quadratic-form order and $\sum_{a}F_{a}=I$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]] clause (a)), the **outcome probabilities** being $p_{a}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})\ge0$, $\sum_{a}p_{a}=1$ by clause (b) of the same lemma. This unsharp extension is an operational description tied to an apparatus model; it is not obtained from the sharp observable by mathematical manipulation alone, and the effects alone do not determine what happens to the state after the outcome (P3). **(v) Moments are a separate matter.** Statements about the mean, variance or higher moments of the outcome law require the corresponding integrability of $t\mapsto t^{n}$ against $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ and are not part of this postulate; where they are used they are stated with their hypotheses. In particular the existence of $\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$ for an unbounded $A$ is not asserted. **(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model. They assert nothing about which quantities of a concrete apparatus are sharp, about the physical mechanism producing an outcome or about the completeness of the description; a laboratory record is a classical event whose relation to the model is a tested identification with uncertainty, in the sense of P7.

**Density operators.** Let $H
e\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $ho$ with $\operatorname{tr}ho=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a) ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). The **state space** of $H$ is the set of all density operators on $H$ and is denoted $$D(H):=\{ho:ho\ 	ext{is a density operator on}\ H\}.$$ An element of $D(H)$ is called a **state** of $H$ in the mathematical sense fixed here. **Pure states.** A state $ho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with $$ho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,uangle u\quad(x\in H),$$ where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map $$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{
u(\psi),
u(\psi)},$$ on the ray space $R(H)$, with $
u$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is $$\widehatho(\psi):= rac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}= rac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$ which equals $T_{
u(\psi),
u(\psi)}$; thus $\widehatho(\psi)$ is the pure state of the ray $[\psi]$, and the vector $\psi$ enters only through its ray. **Purity.** For $ho\in D(H)$ the operator $ho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class: it is self-adjoint by the adjoint algebra of [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], positive because $\langleho^{2}x,xangle=\langleho x,ho xangle\ge0$, and trace class because $ho$ is a bounded trace-class operator and the trace-class operators form a two-sided ideal ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]] clauses 1 and 2). The **purity** of $ho$ is the real number $$\mathcal P(ho):=\operatorname{tr}(ho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$ The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only. **Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Z^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature. **(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres. **(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$; the vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is experimentally determined and $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$. These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]]. **(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities. 1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless. 2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure. 3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$. 4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. 5. Probability current: $j$ has dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$; it is a probability flux, not a charge flux. 6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them. 7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention. 8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list. **(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space $H$ with spectral projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). The **discrete spectrum** $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ is the set of eigenvalues of $A$ that are isolated points of $\sigma(A)$ and whose eigenspace is finite dimensional; the **essential spectrum** is $$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A):=\sigma(A)\setminus\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A),$$ with $\sigma(A)$ as in [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]. For $H=\{0\}$ use its unique PVM directly: the spectrum and both parts are empty and every projection has rank zero. Below suppose $H\ne\{0\}$, as required by the cited spectral theorem. **Spectral-projection description, with proofs.** Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and write $P_\varepsilon:=E((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))$ for $\varepsilon>0$. Here rank means the algebraic dimension of the range when finite; rank $=\infty$ means the range is not finite dimensional. The calculus [[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]] gives the support facts: $E(\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(A))=0$, and every open interval about a spectral point has nonzero projection. Projections on disjoint sets have orthogonal ranges, and $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$ [[def-projection-valued-measure]]. 1. *$E(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection onto $\ker(A-\lambda)$.* If $x=E(\{\lambda\})x$, its scalar measure $E_x$ is supported on $\{\lambda\}$ by the projection identity. Thus $\int\mu^2dE_x=\lambda^2\|x\|^2<\infty$, so $x\in D(A)$, and $$\|(A-\lambda)x\|^2=\int|\mu-\lambda|^2dE_x=0.$$ The domain and norm identities are supplied by the unbounded calculus and [[lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed]]. Hence $Ax=\lambda x$. Conversely, for an eigenvector (or the zero vector) the same norm identity gives zero integral. On $\{|\mu-\lambda|\ge1/n\}$ this bounds the measure by $n^2$ times that zero integral; taking the countable union shows $E_x(\mathbb R\setminus\{\lambda\})=0$. Since $\|(I-E(\{\lambda\}))x\|^2$ equals this scalar measure, $E(\{\lambda\})x=x$. 2. *A finite-rank interval contains only finitely many spectral points.* If $P_\varepsilon$ has rank $r<\infty$ and its interval contained $r+1$ distinct spectral points, choose disjoint small open intervals about those finitely many points, all contained in the given interval. Each has a nonzero projection by support. Choose one unit vector in each range. They are orthonormal vectors in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$, hence linearly independent (take inner products with each vector), contradicting its dimension $r$. Thus there are at most $r$ spectral points there. In particular any $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$ with such a finite-rank $P_\varepsilon$ is isolated: take a smaller interval around $\lambda$ excluding the other finitely many points. For that interval the projection is $E(\{\lambda\})$ by support, is nonzero by support, and has finite rank since its range lies in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$. By item 1, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of finite multiplicity. 3. *The two rank characterizations.* If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$, an isolating interval has projection $E(\{\lambda\})$, of finite rank by item 1. Conversely, if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue and some $P_\varepsilon$ has finite rank, item 2 proves it discrete. Hence $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue and some }P_\varepsilon\text{ has finite rank}.$$ If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, item 2 excludes every finite-rank interval. Conversely, if every $P_\varepsilon$ has infinite rank, each is nonzero, so support puts $\lambda$ in $\sigma(A)$, and the just-proved discrete characterization excludes it from $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$. Therefore $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon=\infty\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0.$$ 4. *$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ is closed.* If $\lambda_n\in \sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ and $\lambda_n\to\lambda$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $n$ has $(\lambda_n-\varepsilon/2, \lambda_n+ \varepsilon/2)\subseteq(\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon)$, so $\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon\ge\operatorname{rank}P_{\varepsilon/2}^{(n)} =\infty$ and $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ by item 3. The closure conclusion is in $\mathbb R$, and also in $\mathbb C$ since $\mathbb R$ is closed there. A spectral accumulation point has infinitely many spectral points in every surrounding interval, so item 2 forces infinite rank. An isolated eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity has its infinite-dimensional eigenspace inside every interval range by item 1. Consequently an accumulation point of $\sigma(A)$ and an isolated eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity both lie in $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, and $\sigma(A)$ is the disjoint union of $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on $(X,\Sigma)$ is a map $$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$ such that: 1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional restriction; 2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$; 3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$; 4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm to $E(B)x$, that is $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$ Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when $X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the $\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite positive measures $$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$ is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page. **Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has $\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so $x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$ for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while $\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives $\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ ([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence $\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties $Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of [[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by [[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$, and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number. **Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and $E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite complex measures, is proved as [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$ Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The **operator norm** of $T$ is $$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$ The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]). In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice principle is used for this assertion. The same number is the least bound of $T$: $$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$ If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives $$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$ When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$, so $\|T\| = 0$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]). **The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.** [[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$. - $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$. - $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values agree. - $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes that $T$ is closable. **Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition. 1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and $\overline T\subseteq T^*$. 2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$, the inclusion reversal of [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$ ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense domain $D(T)$.) 3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal, so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are equalities. 4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$ by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, let $H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and let $H_0:=-\Delta$ be the free operator of [[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]] with domain $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]): $H_0=\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$ and $H_0u=-\Delta u$ for $u\in D(H_0)$, where $\Delta u$ is the distributional Laplacian. Write $M$ for the multiplication operator $$M u:=\frac{u}{|\cdot|},\qquad D(M):=\Bigl\{u\in H:\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\in H\Bigr\},$$ and write $\|u\|_2=\|u\|_H$. Then: (a) for every $u\in D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ one has $u/|\cdot|\in L^2$ and $$\Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le 2\sqrt{\|u\|_2\,\|\Delta u\|_2}\,,\qquad \Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le \eta\|\Delta u\|_2+\frac1\eta\|u\|_2\quad(\eta>0);$$ (b) $M$ is a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with $D(H_0)\subseteq D(M)$, symmetric on $D(H_0)$, with $H_0$-bound zero in the sense that for every $\eta>0$ the pair $(\eta,\eta^{-1})$ is admissible for $M$ relative to $H_0$; (c) for every $\gamma>0$ the operator $$C:=H_0-\gamma M,\qquad D(C):=D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C),$$ is self-adjoint on $H$, bounded below, and acts by $Cu=-\Delta u-\gamma u/|\cdot|$ for every $u\in D(C)$; for every $\eta\in(0,1/\gamma)$ one has $C\ge-\gamma\eta^{-1}/(1-\gamma\eta)$ in the quadratic-form sense. No sharp lower bound of $C$ is claimed here, and no physical interpretation of $C$, $H_0$, $\gamma$ or $\Delta$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Y:=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with its norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]), let $\gamma\in C^2([0,1];(0,\infty))$ with $0<\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma(s)\le\gamma_{\max}<\infty$, and put $$A(s):=-\Delta-\frac{\gamma(s)}{|\cdot|},\qquad D(A(s))=Y .$$ Fix $n\ge1$, let $P_n(s)$ be the spectral projection of $A(s)$ for the eigenvalue $E_n(s)=-\gamma(s)^2/(4n^2)$ and let $g_n:=\inf_{s\in[0,1]}\operatorname{dist}(E_n(s),\sigma(A(s))\setminus\{E_n(s)\})>0$ be the uniform gap to the rest of the spectrum. Let $U_T$ solve $i\,\partial_sU_T=T A(s)U_T$, $U_T(0)=I$ ([[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-common-domain-nonautonomous-evolution]], with $T$ a slow-time parameter). Then there is a constant $C<\infty$, depending on $n,\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}$ and the $C^2$ norm of $\gamma$, with $$\bigl\|(I-P_n(s))U_T(s)P_n(0)\bigr\|\le\frac CT,\qquad s\in[0,1].$$ The theorem is a conditional statement about the external-source Coulomb family $A(s)$; no laboratory control field, error rate or physical preparation is asserted, and linear Stark-type couplings are not covered.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]). (a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two. (b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$. (c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$ where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

derivations.claim: [Common domain and automatic regularity] Put $B=-\Delta$, $Mu=u/|x|$ and $\gamma_{\max}=2m\kappa_{\max}/\hbar^2$. By [F6], each $A(s)=B-\gamma(s)M$ is self-adjoint on exactly the dense Hilbert domain $Y=H^2$, continuously embedded in $L^2$. Choose $\eta=(2\gamma_{\max})^{-1}$. For every $u\in Y$, $\gamma(s)\|Mu\|_2\le\tfrac12\|Bu\|_2+2\gamma_{\max}^2\|u\|_2$, whence $\|A(s)u\|_2\le\tfrac32\|Bu\|_2+2\gamma_{\max}^2\|u\|_2$ and $\|Bu\|_2\le2\|A(s)u\|_2+4\gamma_{\max}^2\|u\|_2$. Together with the fixed Fourier/Sobolev equivalence of [F6], these give uniform equivalence between $\|u\|_Y$ and $\|u\|_2+\|A(s)u\|_2$. Also $M:Y\to L^2$ is bounded, by the same estimate, so $A\in C^2([0,1];\mathcal B(Y,L^2))$ with $A'=-\gamma'M$ and $A''=-\gamma''M$. All these norms are controlled by $\gamma_{\max}$ and $\|\gamma\|_{C^2}$. Positive multiplication by $\hbar^2/(2m)$ gives the same exact domain and uniform graph equivalence for $H(s)$ and yields $H'=-\kappa'M$, $H''=-\kappa''M$. Thus every stated positive $C^2$ path automatically satisfies branch (u); [F3] supplies the unique domain-preserving unitary propagator for the self-adjoint $C^1$ family $T H(s)/\hbar$ on $Y$. [given, F1, F3, F6, algebra]

[Correct adjacent gaps and the whole level] By [F1] and [F2], $H(s)=(\hbar^2/(2m))A(s)$ has eigenvalues exactly $E_n(s)=-(\hbar^2/(2m))\gamma(s)^2/(4n^2)$, each eigenspace having dimension $n^2$; its nonnegative spectrum is the essential interval $[0,\infty)$ and contains no eigenvalue. Since $E_1<E_2<\cdots<0$, the complementary distance at $E_n$ is the minimum of the positive differences $E_{n+1}-E_n$, $E_n-E_{n-1}$ when $n\ge2$, and $|E_n|$. Dividing by $(\hbar^2/(2m))\gamma(s)^2$ gives, respectively, $\delta_n=(2n+1)/(4n^2(n+1)^2)$, $(2n-1)/(4n^2(n-1)^2)$ and $1/(4n^2)$. The first is the smallest: $2n+1\le(n+1)^2$, and $(2n-1)(n+1)^2-(2n+1)(n-1)^2=6n^2-2>0$ for $n\ge2$. Hence the distance is exactly $(\hbar^2/(2m))\gamma(s)^2\delta_n\ge g_n>0$. For the normalized family $A(s)$ this gives the uniform bound $\widetilde g_n=\delta_n\gamma_{\min}^2>0$, with $g_n=(\hbar^2/(2m))\widetilde g_n$. The eigenprojection refers to the entire $n^2$-dimensional space; no vector or sublevel is selected. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

[Projection regularity and coherent local Riesz following] Write $e_n(s)=-\gamma(s)^2/(4n^2)$, $\rho=\widetilde g_n/3$ and $z(s,\theta)=e_n(s)+\rho e^{i\theta}$. Step 2.1 gives spectral distance at least $\rho$ on this circle. The exact-domain resolvent $R(s,\theta)=(z(s,\theta)-A(s))^{-1}$ therefore has $L^2$ norm at most $\rho^{-1}$ by the contour/PVM argument in [F6]. The identity $A(s)R=zR-I$ and step 1.1's uniform graph bound give a uniform $L^2\to Y$ bound, since $z$ is uniformly bounded by the path data. Put $B_j(s)=A^{(j)}(s)-e_n^{(j)}(s)I:Y\to L^2$ for $j=1,2$. The inverse equations on these exact spaces give joint continuity and $C^2$ regularity in $s$ by the local Neumann identity; differentiating gives $R'=RB_1R$ and $R''=RB_2R+2RB_1RB_1R$ in $\mathcal B(L^2,Y)$. These derivatives are uniformly bounded by the established bounds and $\|\gamma\|_{C^2}$. Thus $P_n(s)=(\rho/(2\pi))\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i\theta}R(s,\theta)\,d\theta$ is $C^2$ in $\mathcal B(L^2,Y)$; the PVM contour formula of [F6] identifies this integral with the full eigenprojection, and positive energy scaling leaves that eigenspace and projection unchanged. For any $s_0$, continuity of $e_n$ gives a neighborhood with $|e_n(s)-e_n(s_0)|<\rho/2$. The fixed circle $|z-e_n(s_0)|=\rho$ then encloses $e_n(s)$ and excludes the rest of the spectrum, whose distance from its center is at least $\widetilde g_n-\rho/2>\rho$. Its resolvents have the same local $C^2$ inverse construction, and its Riesz integral is exactly $P_n(s)$. On overlapping neighborhoods the integrals agree as the same named spectral projection. Therefore $P_n$ is norm-continuous and coincides with coherent local Riesz continuation from $P_n(0)$ in [F4], proving the final assertion of (a). [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F2, F4, F6, construct, algebra]

[Rescaling the supplier] By [F1] the family $A(s)$ satisfies the hypotheses of [F3] with $\gamma_{\min}=2m\kappa_{\min}/\hbar^{2}$ and $\gamma_{\max}=2m\kappa_{\max}/\hbar^{2}$, and by step 2.1 the normalized named eigenvalue has the uniform gap $\widetilde g_n>0$, with coherent $C^2$ projection supplied by step 3.1, so [F3] supplies a constant $C<\infty$ with the normalized bound $\|(I-P_{n}(s))U^{A}_{S}(s)P_{n}(0)\|\le C/S$, where $U^{A}_{S}$ solves $i\partial_{s}U^{A}_{S}=SA(s)U^{A}_{S}$. The physical family is $H(s)=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}A(s)$, so the physical equation $i\hbar\partial_{s}U_{T}=TH(s)U_{T}$ is $i\partial_{s}U_{T}=\frac{T\hbar}{2m}A(s)U_{T}$; hence $U_{T}=U^{A}_{S}$ with $S=\frac{T\hbar}{2m}$ and the normalized bound becomes $\|(I-P_{n}(s))U_{T}(s)P_{n}(0)\|\le 2mC/(\hbar T)$. Setting $C_{n}:=\frac{2mC}{\hbar}$ (seconds; finite, depending only on $n,m,\hbar$ and the path data through $\gamma$) gives the operator bound of clause (b). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F3, algebra]

[Born leakage and survival] Let $\psi(0)\in\operatorname{ran}P_{n}(0)$ be unit, so $P_{n}(0)\psi(0)=\psi(0)$; $U_{T}(s,0)$ is unitary, so $\psi(sT)$ is unit, and $(I-P_{n}(s))\psi(sT)=(I-P_{n}(s))U_{T}(s,0)P_{n}(0)\psi(0)$; the operator bound of step 4.1 and [F5] give $\|(I-P_{n}(s))\psi(sT)\|\le C_{n}/T$, whose square is $p_{\mathrm{leak}}(s)$ by [F4], and the survival probability is $1-p_{\mathrm{leak}}(s)\ge1-C_{n}^{2}/T^{2}$ by [F5]. This is clause (b). [step 4.1, F4, F5, algebra]

[Supported mixed preparations] Let $\rho_0=P_n(0)\rho_0P_n(0)$. In the expansion of [F7], every vector of positive eigenvalue $w_j$ satisfies $u_j=w_j^{-1}\rho_0u_j\in\operatorname{ran}P_n(0)$.
